Complainant

A-2) Sh. Harmeet Singh

R/o. B-33, Gujranwala Town, Delhi- 09
A-3) M/s. Uttam Singh & Sons
9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07 ...

Accused Persons
Judgment:

1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules

. 
The accused no.1 (since expired) and accused no.2 are stated to be the partners of accused no.3 partnership firm that that supplied the food article, that is, 'Tea' to the vendor Sh. Satya Dev Gupta from whom it was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 16.05.2006, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Gian Chand and Field Assistant (FA) J. P. Bhardwaj under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Yogesh Pratap reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Shyam Cigarrette Store at 18A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi - 07, where one Sh. Satya Dev Gupta was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Tea from the vendor as lying in sealed pouches of 250 gram each bearing identical label declaration and In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
1 batch number, to which he agreed.
A sample of three such packets of Tea was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened,
marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 24.05.2006, the PA found the sample to be 'misbranded' because the language of best before declaration was not as per Rule 32(i) of PFA Rules.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.

Investigation revealed that the vendor Satya Dev Gupta was the proprietor of M/s. Shyam Cigarette Store, who had purchased the food article from M/s. Uttam Singh & Sons (accused no.3 partnership firm herein).
The said partnership firm was having two partners i.e. Sh. Harmeet Singh (accused no.2 herein) and Sh. Uttam Singh (accused no.1 herein, since expired).

It was further found that the food article had been manufactured / packed by a company M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt.
Ltd., of which Sh. Harmeet Singh (accused no.2 herein) and Sh. Ramneet Singh were the Directors.

sentences.text: 3. At the time of lifting of sample, there was a policy of the complainant department bearing no.F6(228)/85/ENF./PFA dated 23.09.1985 according to which no prosecution was to be launched against first violators of Rule 32 and instead, only a warning in writing was to be issued.
Though the said policy was subsequently withdrawn vide office order no.5/07 dated 14.09.2007, yet the said policy was in operation on the day of lifting the sample.
4. The investigation revealed that the vendor Satya Dev Gupta, the manufacturing company M/s.
Uttam Singh

Tea Company Pvt. Ltd., and its Directors Sh. Harmeet Singh (accused no. 2 herein) and Sh. Ramneet Singh were the first violators of Rule 32 and in compliance with the above policy, a warning was issued to them and no prosecution was launched against them.

However, it was found that Sh. Harmeet Singh (accused no.2 herein in the capacity of partner) along with the partnership firm accused no.3 had already been issued a warning vide letter no. F- 6(901)/94/PFA/7420-21 dated 29.09.2004 by the LHA.
As the said firm and its partners were not the first violators of Rule 32, they were not entitled to the benefit of policy.
Thus, after completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 01.09.2006 against the supplier firm accused no.3 and its two partners accused no.1 and 2, alleging violation of section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rule 32(i) of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
5. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 01.09.2006.
6. Accused no.1 expired during the pendency of the case on 13.05.2009 and proceedings against him stood abated, as per order dated 05.04.2010.

Based on the report of PA, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against the accused no.2 and 3 vide order dated 13.08.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
2 7.
At the trial, prosecution examined four witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 FI Sh. Gian Chan,
PW-2 Sh. Yogesh Pratap (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA J. P. Bhardwaj were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 16.05.2006 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed packets of Tea (Uttam brand) of 250 gram each, dividing it in three parts after considering one packet as one counterpart, fastening, sealing, marking the sample counterparts, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B,
Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, Notice under section 14A Ex. PW-1/D, Raid Report Ex. PW-1/D-1, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex. PW- 1/F.
PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received and investigation was conducted by PW-1 who sent letter Ex. PW-1/H to the vendor and received its reply Ex. PW-1/H-1 along with some documents.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/I to VAT Officer and received its reply.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/J to accused no.3 and received its reply Ex. PW-1/J along with copy of the bill and other documents.
Letter Ex. PW-1/K was written to the STO and the particulars of the partners of accused no.3 were ascertained.
Similarly, letter Ex. PW-1/K-1 was sent to STO to ascertain the constitution of the manufacturing company and its reply was received.
Letter Ex. PW-1/K-2 was also sent to the said company which was replied vide letter Ex. PW- 1/K-3 thereby confirming the sale of food article to accused no.3 herein vide bill no. 32 dated 06.05.2006.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/L was taken from the Director PFA and thereafter, complaint Ex. PW-1/M was filed in the court.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/N was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/O.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by the Ld. Defence Counsel for accused no.2 and 3 wherein they denied that no previous warning was served upon the accused persons.
8. The complainant also examined PW-4 Sh. R. P. Singh who produced the record of issuance of warning letter to accused no.2 and 3 on 29.09.1994 by the then LHA Sh. R. K. Ahuja.
Copy of the same Ex. PW- 4/A and dak register Ex. PW-4/B were proved.
9. Statement of the accused no.2 (also representing accused no.3 firm as its AR) under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 22.09.2014 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
He expressed ignorance about the sample proceedings, though questioned the PA report claiming that there was no misbranding.
He stated that no warning letter was ever issued to him and also alleged that the vendor might be selling spurious / duplicate products.
He chose to lead evidence in defence.

10. The accused persons summoned the record of telephone bill from MTNL through DW-1 Sh.
Rajinder Singh.
He proved the record Ex. DW- 1/A and Ex. DW-1/B, where the address of accused no. 1 was mentioned as "Shop No. 6313, 9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07".
Similarly, record of electricity bill Ex. DW-2/A to Ex. DW-2/D was proved by DW-2 Sh. S. S. Negi from TPDDL.
Record of MCD was also proved as Ex. DW-3/A through DW-3 Sh. Shivender Singh.

11. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt as all the witnesses have supported its case and no material contradiction can be seen in their testimonies.

It In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
3 is submitted that the accused persons have failed to rebut the findings of the PA report which shows that the sample was misbranded being in violation of the packaging and labelling rules.
It is also contended that the record clearly establishes that the accused persons were not the first violators and are thus liable to be prosecuted.
12. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has argued that no case is made out against the accused persons.
Ld. Counsel has submitted that date of packing was given on the label and therefore, the best before declaration could be ascertained easily without any problem.

It is thus contended that there is no violation of Rule 32(i) because the words "best before 12 months" read together with the declaration "month and year packed- 3/06" would be sufficient to convey the meaning, even if the exact language of Rule 32(i) "best before 12 months from packaging / manufacture" was not used.

It is then submitted that the accused persons had never received and previous warning as per the policy of the complainant and therefore, they were also entitled to be given warning in writing instead of launching the prosecution.
13.
I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant as well as Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused no.2 and 3 and have carefully perused the material available on record.
14. It is to be understood that the present is a case of misbranding with respect to violation of packaging and labelling rules as provided under the PFA Rules.
The quality of the product in question was found to be as per the prescribed standards and there is no violation of any rules pertaining to quality, substance and nature of the product.
There is no allegation of any kind of adulteration in the food article on any of the parameters provided under section 2(ia) of the PFA Act.
15. The case of the complainant is based on the report of the PA Ex. PW-1/G wherein she opined the sample to be 'misbranded' on account of violation of Rules 32(i) of PFA Rules.

It was observed by the PA that the Best Before Date was declared without reference to the Date of Packing /
Manufacturing and thus, the language of Best Before Declaration was not as per Rule 32(i).
16. The accused persons have not questioned the label declarations as reproduced by the FI on Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B.
It is not their case that the said declarations were not reproduced correctly by the FI or that some portion was omitted by the FI or that some portion was incorrectly written therein.

For that matter, they have also not questioned the findings of the PA to the effect that the package in question was having the Best Before Declaration without reference to the Date of Packing / Manufacturing.

17. I do not find merit in the stand of Ld. Defence Counsel that the declaration given on the label conveys the same meaning as required by the PFA Rules.
18.

In the judgement titled as Ram Babu Rastogi v. State [2012 (1) FAC 56 (Delhi High Court)], the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held that the objective of declaration on the label was that the purchaser should know at the time of purchase, as to whether the article, which is purchased was capable of being as used and till what time.

entities.text: Ram Babu Rastogi v. State [2012 (1) FAC 56 (Delhi High Court)]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Hon'ble High Court was dealing with a position In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
4 where the actual label of the sample was "Best Before within 6 months from the date of packing" as against the required language "Best Before 6 months from the date of packing".
It was held that the language so used conveyed much more than what was required to be conveyed to the purchaser about the genuineness of the product.

It was held that mere use of the word "within" as a surplusage would not bring the petitioners under the penal provisions of the Act, as by any means, the purchasers could not be said to have been deceived or misled as regards the character, quantity,
quality, or date of manufacture and the limit of use of the product.

Observing that the word "within"
stood omitted after 01.09.2011, it was held that merely by adding such a word, no customer could be said to have been misled or misdirected as there was no difference otherwise in the meaning conveyed.
Therefore, the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi quashed the proceedings in that matter.
19. But the present case stands on different footing altogether.
It is not the use of words "if" or "within" that only have been changed, rather it is the completing phrase as well that has been omitted by the accused persons on the label.
In simple words, the accused persons have failed to mention that the twelve months period would be from the date of packaging/manufacturing.

In the absence of these words, it would be definitely not ascertainable by a prospective purchaser as to if the twelve months period would be from the date of packing/manufacturing, or from the date of sale of the product, or from the date of opening the seal of the packet.
It shall not be possible for the court to assume that every person who purchases such product would be certain that this date has to be construed as the date of packing.
From this angle, the language used on the label would be misleading and incomplete.

It is to be noted that to reach such a conclusion, the court has to look at the things from the eyes of an ordinary person who may not be versed in the technicalities of language or legal provisions, and not from the eyes of a well educated and qualified luminary.

Such an ordinary person can be easily misled by such language used on labelling by telling him that the product would remain fresh for twelve months after breaking open its seal, irrespective of the date of packing mentioned thereupon.

And the accused persons have failed to explain why and for what purpose the language as required by the rules was altered / modified / changed, particularly when the other declarations were as per the PFA Rules.

20. Same was the position in the judgements titled as Nehrudasan v. Food Inspector, Madurai [2010(1) FAC 49 (Madras High Court)], A. Rajasingh v. Food Inspector [2008(1) FAC 172 (Madras High Court)], T. Prabhu v. The Madras State [2007(1) FAC 314 (Madras High Court)] and Hindustan Lever Limited v. Food Inspector [2007(1) FAC 299 (Madras High Court)].

sentences.text: In all these cases, it was clearly mentioned on the labels that the best before period was from the date of packing / manufacturing and it was only the use or omission of some word in the language that had not made any material difference in the sense being conveyed.
But in the present case, there is material omission and the sense being conveyed is prone to be misused against the consumer.
These judgements would therefore not come to the rescue of the accused persons.
21. The language used by the accused persons in this case, that is, "Best before 12 months" would be therefore not in conformity with the language of Rule 32(i).

It would have been fine if the accused had mentioned "Best before 12 months from the date of packing" OR "Best before 3/07", but in this case, no such specific date has been mentioned by the accused persons with respect to the best before date.

In the present case, it is not mentioned that twelve months period has to be calculated In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
5 from the date of packing only.

entities.text: Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 22. Thus, such omission has tendency to cause prejudice to the purchaser / customer who might purchase the packet in question.

The consumer might get confused or might be misled in ascertaining if the said period of twelve months would be from the date of packaging as mentioned on the label or from the date of purchase or from the date of opening the seal of the packet.
There is no merit in the stand that the language used would not create confusion in view of the date of packing mentioned on the label.

If that was so, there was no need for the authorities to prescribe and frame specific and precise rules and at the same time, there was no need for the accused to have changed the language on his labels in violation of these rules.
It would be for the accused to explain why he failed to use the prescribed language when he was aware that some such requirement was there under the rules.
If the meaning conveyed was supposed to be the same, there was no reason for him to cause damage to the prescribed language to such extent.

It is apparent that there is violation of Rule 32(i) of PFA Rules in this matter and consequently section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act.
23.

There is no force in the claim of the accused that the vendor might have been selling spurious /
duplicate products under the name and style of M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd., as claimed by him for the first time in his statement under section 313 CrPC.

entities.text: Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: No such stand was taken at the trial nor any such suggest was put to any PW so as to give them an opportunity to affirm or deny or dispute the said stand.

No attempt was made by the accused persons to call for the remaining counterparts from the office of the LHA so as to compare the same with the actual label manufactured by the company so as to ascertain if the said food articles were spurious or duplicate.

Again, the said claim of the accused no.2 (also on behalf of accused no.3) would be in contradiction to his reply given to the FI vide letter Ex. PW-1/J-1 dated 09.06.2006, wherein in the capacity of the partner of accused no.3, he confirmed the sale of sampled commodity to the vendor vide invoice dated 16.05.2006.

Similarly, the said claim of the accused no.2 (also on behalf of accused no.3)
would also be in contradiction to his reply given to the FI vide letter Ex. PW-1/K-3 dated 05.07.2006, wherein in the capacity of Director of the manufacturing company M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd., he confirmed the sale of sampled commodity to the accused no.3 herein vide bill no. 32 dated 06.05.2006.

entities.text: Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: In view of the said material, there is no merit in such a defence raised by the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC, particularly when no such defence has been proved by leading suitable evidence in defence.
24. The accused persons have tried to raise a defence that no previous warning letter was issued to or served upon them.

The three DWs have been examined to show that the correct and complete address was "6313, 9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07" and that the address "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07"
was incomplete.
25. However, even such a stand is not justifiable.

Even if the records produced by the three DWs are accepted to be correct, yet there is nothing to show that the address "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07" at which the intimation letters had been sent, was incomplete or incorrect so as to make it impossible for the letters to be served.
The original record of sending the letter has been proved by PW-4 and there is nothing to show that the same is false and fabricated, as suggested by the defence.
The dak register Ex. PW-4/B would show that the warning letters were sent at "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07".

In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
6
As far as this address is concern, it was disclosed by the vendor on Form VI Ex. PW-1/B.
The bill Mark- X, which has been accepted by the accused no.2 to be correct in his reply Ex. PW-1/J-1, also mentions the address of accused no.3 as "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07".

Apparently, the accused no.
2 used a very old letter head in giving the reply dated 09.06.2006 Ex. PW-1/J-1 (where the phone numbers appear in seven digits, the paper quality is very old and the address of the shop as it existed at that time is mentioned).

Still, when the bill Mark- X dated 16.05.2006 has been admitted, it is clear that even the address appearing on the invoice of accused no. 3, that is, "9A, Kamla Nagar,
Delhi- 07" was correct and complete.
Again, the notice Ex. PW-1/D was issued by the FI to the accused no.3 at this very address.
The fact that accused no.2 gave reply Ex. PW-1/J-1 to this notice would show that the said letter of the FI was duly served upon him at this very address.

Further, the bill Mark- X3, which has been accepted by the accused no.2 (in the capacity of Director of the manufacturing company) to be correct in his reply Ex. PW-1/K-3, also mentions the address of accused no.3 as "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07".

Therefore, accused no.2, who was partner of accused no.3 and also Director of the manufacturing company, has throughout accepted the correctness of the address at which the warning letters had been sent.
Moreover, the summons of the court were also sent at the same address and duly served upon the accused persons.
Even in his bail bond, the accused no.2 gave his address as "9A, Kamla Nagar, Delhi- 07".
Thus, it does not lie in his mouth to now dispute the correctness of this address.

In view of the testimony of PW-4 coupled with the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act and also the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, it has been established that warnings had been issued to the accused persons previously and deemed to be served.
It was for the accused persons to rebut the said presumptions but they have failed to do so.
26. Despite arriving at such a finding, one more important point is to be considered, which has never been sufficiently raised by the defence either at the trial or at the stage of arguments.

27. As per Section 14 of PFA Act, no manufacturer or distributor of or dealer in any article of food shall sell such article to any vendor unless he also gives a warranty in writing in the prescribed form about the nature and quality of such article to the vendor.

28. Section 19(2) of PFA Act provides that a vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded article of food if he proves that he had purchased the food article from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer with a written warranty in the prescribed form, and that the said article of food while in his possession was properly stored and that he sold it in the same state as he purchased it.
29.

Further, as per the proviso to Section 14 of PFA Act (inserted in 1976), a bill, cash memorandum or invoice in respect of the sale of any article of food given by a manufacturer or distributor of or dealer in such article to the vendor thereof shall be deemed to be a warranty given by such manufacturer, distributor or dealer under the said section.
30. Though the vendor Satya Dev Gupta has not been prosecuted on account of policy of the department, yet he would have been governed by the concept of warranty as per section 19(2) of PFA Act.

He had relied upon the bill dated 16.05.2006 issued by accused no.3, copy of which is Mark- X,
In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
7 the genuineness of which has never been disputed and rather admitted by accused no.2 and 3 in their reply dated 09.06.2006 Ex. PW- 1/J-1.
They have categorically confirmed the "sale" of "sampled commodity" to Shyam Cigarette Store vide "invoice dated 16.05.2006".
It is not the case of the FI that the said document is forged or fabricated.
It is not the case of the prosecution that the food article lifted for sampling was not connected with the food article sold through this bill.
In that case, there was no occasion for the FI to implicate the accused no.3 at all.
31. In my considered view, the same rule should apply even to accused no.3 as well.
Even the accused no.3 (and consequently accused no.2 in the capacity of its partner) would also be governed by the concept of warranty as per Section 19(2) of PFA Act.

Even the accused no.3 (through accused no.2) in its reply Ex. PW-1/J-1 dated 09.06.2006 had relied upon the invoice no. 32 dated 06.05.2006 issued by the manufacturing company M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd. (which along with its Directors has also not been prosecuted due to existence of policy), copy of which is Mark- X3, the genuineness of which has never been disputed and rather admitted by the said company M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd. in its reply dated 05.07.2006 Ex. PW-1/K-3 (given by accused no.2 herein but in the capacity of Director of the said company).

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Even the said company has categorically confirmed the "sale" of "sampled Tea" to M/s. Uttam Singh & Sons (accused no.3 herein) vide "bill no. 32, dated 06.05.2006".
Again, it is not the case of the FI that the said document is forged or fabricated.
It is also not the case of the prosecution that the food article lifted for sampling was not connected with the food article sold through this bill.
In that case, there was no occasion for the FI to issue warning to the said manufacturing company or its Directors.
32. It is to be understood that a company is a separate legal entity distinct from its Directors.
Accused no.2 herein was a partner of M/s. Uttam Singh & Sons (partnership firm) and also a Director of M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd., (a private limited company).

entities.text: Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Even as per the complaint Ex. PW-1/M, warning was issued to the said company and also its Directors including accused no.2 herein, though accused no.2 was prosecuted in the capacity of partner of the accused no.3 firm on the ground that they have been given warnings previously.
Thus, despite the fact that accused no.2 was in receipt of warning earlier, he had received the same in different capacity as partner of a firm and not in the capacity of the Director of a company.
The said warning cannot be taken as a warning given previously to the company.

Precisely for this reason, the FI did not implicate the accused no.2 in the capacity of the Director of the manufacturing company and implicated him only being the partner of accused no.3.
33.
It is also clear that the food article was sold in the same condition as purchased.
It is rather an admitted position that the food article was lying in sealed packets as packed by the manufacturer.
There is no allegation that the vendor or supplier had altered or manipulated the seals.

Going by the proviso to section 14 of the PFA Act, the bill relied upon by the vendor (as accepted and confirmed by the supplier and not disputed even by the prosecution) would give him the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) PFA Act.

Similarly, the bill relied upon by the supplier / distributor (accused no.
3 herein) (as accepted and confirmed by the manufacturer and not disputed even by the prosecution) would give it (and consequently its partners) the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) PFA Act.

This benefit of warranty would not have been available to the manufacturing company or persons incharge of responsible to it for its affairs, because it had not procured it from In Re vs A-1) Sh. Uttam Singh on 20 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75769972/
8 some other person so as to be covered by section 19(2) of PFA Act.

But no prosecution has been launched against the said company or its directors, due to existence of policy of the complainant,
which has been recognized by the High Court of Delhi in S. S. Gokul Krishnan v. State [2009(1) FAC 132] and other precedents.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 34. In view of this discussion, the accused no. 3 (and consequently the accused no. 2 in the capacity of its partner) is given the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) read with section 14 of the PFA Act.
Both the accused no. 2 and 3 are therefore acquitted of the charges.

35. Bail bond of accused no. 2 shall however remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A CrPC.
36.
File be consigned to the record room.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
14. It is to be understood that the present is a case of misbranding with respect to violation of packaging and labelling rules as provided under the PFA Rules.
The quality of the product in question was found to be as per the prescribed standards and there is no violation of any rules pertaining to quality, substance and nature of the product.
There is no allegation of any kind of adulteration in the food article on any of the parameters provided under section 2(ia) of the PFA Act.
In simple words, the accused persons have failed to mention that the twelve months period would be from the date of packaging/manufacturing.
In the absence of these words, it would be definitely not ascertainable by a prospective purchaser as to if the twelve months period would be from the date of packing/manufacturing, or from the date of sale of the product, or from the date of opening the seal of the packet.
It shall not be possible for the court to assume that every person who purchases such product would be certain that this date has to be construed as the date of packing.
It is to be noted that to reach such a conclusion, the court has to look at the things from the eyes of an ordinary person who may not be versed in the technicalities of language or legal provisions, and not from the eyes of a well educated and qualified luminary.
Such an ordinary person can be easily misled by such language used on labelling by telling him that the product would remain fresh for twelve months after breaking open its seal, irrespective of the date of packing mentioned thereupon.
And the accused persons have failed to explain why and for what purpose the language as required by the rules was altered / modified / changed, particularly when the other declarations were as per the PFA Rules.
20. Same was the position in the judgements titled as Nehrudasan v. Food Inspector, Madurai [2010(1) FAC 49 (Madras High Court)], A. Rajasingh v. Food Inspector [2008(1) FAC 172 (Madras High Court)], T. Prabhu v. The Madras State [2007(1) FAC 314 (Madras High Court)] and Hindustan Lever Limited v. Food Inspector [2007(1) FAC 299 (Madras High Court)].
In all these cases, it was clearly mentioned on the labels that the best before period was from the date of packing / manufacturing and it was only the use or omission of some word in the language that had not made any material difference in the sense being conveyed.
But in the present case, there is material omission and the sense being conveyed is prone to be misused against the consumer.
21. The language used by the accused persons in this case, that is, "Best before 12 months" would be therefore not in conformity with the language of Rule 32(i).
It would have been fine if the accused had mentioned "Best before 12 months from the date of packing" OR "Best before 3/07", but in this case, no such specific date has been mentioned by the accused persons with respect to the best before date.
22. Thus, such omission has tendency to cause prejudice to the purchaser / customer who might purchase the packet in question.
The consumer might get confused or might be misled in ascertaining if the said period of twelve months would be from the date of packaging as mentioned on the label or from the date of purchase or from the date of opening the seal of the packet.
There is no merit in the stand that the language used would not create confusion in view of the date of packing mentioned on the label.
If that was so, there was no need for the authorities to prescribe and frame specific and precise rules and at the same time, there was no need for the accused to have changed the language on his labels in violation of these rules.
It would be for the accused to explain why he failed to use the prescribed language when he was aware that some such requirement was there under the rules.
If the meaning conveyed was supposed to be the same, there was no reason for him to cause damage to the prescribed language to such extent.
It is apparent that there is violation of Rule 32(i) of PFA Rules in this matter and consequently section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act.
23.
There is no force in the claim of the accused that the vendor might have been selling spurious /
duplicate products under the name and style of M/s. Uttam Singh Tea Company Pvt. Ltd., as claimed by him for the first time in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
In view of the testimony of PW-4 coupled with the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act and also the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, it has been established that warnings had been issued to the accused persons previously and deemed to be served.
It was for the accused persons to rebut the said presumptions but they have failed to do so.
But no prosecution has been launched against the said company or its directors, due to existence of policy of the complainant,
which has been recognized by the High Court of Delhi in S. S. Gokul Krishnan v. State [2009(1) FAC 132] and other precedents.
